No page gives a usable skip test. Pages either say 'always do discovery' (vendors) or list skip cases in prose (logrocket, dualboot FAQ). A scored yes/no test with three outcomes (skip, light, full) is missing.

outline.h2: Is a discovery phase worth it for a new product?
outline.answerHint: Start with 'Yes.' Yes for a new product when at least one core assumption (who the user is, what job they hire it for, whether they will pay, whether they can use it) has no evidence yet; no when the product repeats a proven one and the evidence already exists. Then the definition in one line: design-led discovery is the first 2 steps of a digital product design engagement, before anyone designs screens.
points: Define the discovery phase in this post's sense: discovery and product strategy plus user research, steps 1-2 of the hub process. Link UP to the hub early: [digital product design services](/services/digital-product-design-services/).

Frame 'worth it' as risk bought down: value, usability, business viability and feasibility (the four big risks, cite SVPG). Discovery buys down the first three with evidence; feasibility input comes from your engineers.
GOV.UK Service Manual: discovery is about understanding the problem before committing to build, and the team does not build during it. Cite it as the public-sector standard, not as startup data.
Close the section with the reader's next step: the 6-question test below.

outline.h2: What does a discovery phase hand to your design team?
outline.answerHint: Bold answer: 4 outputs the design work starts from, a 1-page product brief, a research report, a sitemap with user flows and a set of success metrics. Each is something a designer uses on day 1 of the prototype.
points: Product brief: target users, Jobs to be Done, success metrics (hub example: weekly active users, task completion time), set with the Google HEART framework.
Research report: 5-8 interviews per user group, findings such as unmet needs, current workarounds and switching triggers (hub wording). Synthesized in Dovetail per the hub.
Sitemap and user flows for every core task: the input to the clickable prototype that step 4 tests with 5 users per round in Maze.
Contrast with what development-agency discovery hands over (tech stack, estimates). Keep it neutral and do not claim what the agency does or does not build (see notes).
Visual: output stack infographic, text behind 'Show as text'.

outline.h2: Which assumptions should discovery test before design starts?
outline.answerHint: Bold answer: the ones that would change the product if wrong, sorted into value, usability and viability, each with the method that tests it and the evidence that counts.
points: Assumption ledger: assumption -> risk type -> method (stakeholder interviews, Jobs to be Done interviews, competitor review, prototype test) -> evidence bar (what counts as confirmed).
Worked rows from a hypothetical product, labelled illustrative (e.g. 'clinic managers will switch from spreadsheets'). Do not use client names here.
Rank by 'how bad if wrong' x 'how little evidence' and test the top 3 first. Tell the reader to list their riskiest 3 now, because the closing CTA asks for them.
Visual: assumption ledger table as an infographic (text behind 'Show as text').

outline.h2: When can you skip a discovery phase?
outline.answerHint: Bold answer: when you can answer yes to most of 6 questions about evidence you already hold. 0-2 yes means run full discovery, 3-4 means a light version, 5-6 means skip it and start design.
points: The 6 questions (yes/no): 1) Have you interviewed at least 5 target users about this problem in the last 12 months? 2) Can you name the one job users hire the product for? 3) Do you know what users use today and why they would switch? 4) Is there a paying customer, signed pilot or waitlist for this exact product? 5) Are the success metrics set and agreed by the founders? 6) Is the scope fixed by something outside your control (regulation, a contract, a platform rule)?
State that the thresholds are our rule of thumb from running engagements, not research data.

Light version for 3-4 yes: a 5-day design sprint that tests 1 value proposition. This is the ONE cross-hub link: [UI UX design services for startups](/services/ui-ux-design-services-for-startups/). Do not restate that page's price or deliverables.

Honest skip cases: a rebuild of a product whose users you already study, an internal tool with 1 known user group, a scope set by regulation. Say plainly that discovery is then a cost with little return.
Visual: skip-test decision flow (6 questions -> 3 outcomes).

outline.h2: What does skipping discovery cost you later?
outline.answerHint: Bold answer: the same wrong assumption gets found later and costs more each time, first in a prototype test (design hours), then in build (development sprints), then after launch (users who leave). Reason from the hub's rework logic, not vendor percentages.
points: Ladder: where a wrong assumption surfaces: interview -> prototype test -> build sprint -> after launch. Hub benefit card wording: issues found in a clickable prototype cost hours to fix, after launch they cost development sprints.
GOV.UK: discovery can end in a decision not to move on to the next phase. Present 'stop' as a cheap, good outcome: the cheapest product to cancel is the one with no code.

Optional, only if the fact-checker can confirm the current figure on cbinsights.com: CB Insights' post-mortem analysis lists 'no market need' among the top reasons startups fail. Use the figure from the CB Insights page itself, with its year, or leave it out (secondary sources disagree: 42% in the 2014 version, 35% in a later update).
Do NOT use vendor percentages (see notes).
Visual: 'where a wrong assumption surfaces' ladder, qualitative (no invented cost multipliers).

outline.h2: What did discovery settle for Nitro League, Vocable and Digno?
outline.answerHint: Bold answer: in all three idea-to-product projects, discovery fixed who the product serves and how its core logic works before visual design started. One short paragraph per case, facts only from the case-study files, each with a DOWN link.
points: Nitro League (/case-studies/nitro/): one product for gamers, NFT collectors and investors; started with product discovery and stakeholder interviews; from these the team mapped the user flows and wrote a detailed whitepaper; branding workshops followed; professional gamers validated the result. Reported result: secured $5M in funding within 3 months. Do not attribute the funding to discovery alone.

Vocable (/case-studies/vocable/): scope included stakeholder interviews and an MVP launch strategy; the team mapped the full creator journey and designed each screen around a problem heard in stakeholder interviews (planning, drafting, optimizing, publishing). Reported results: 35% increase in overall workflow efficiency, 20% improvement in content quality and consistency.

Digno (/case-studies/digno/): the team gathered requirements from different stakeholders and users to define how the score is calculated, and studied competitors that had tried to solve similar problems; that research shaped 5 core experiences. Quote at most one result exactly as written ('5x increase in overall revenue'), labelled as the case study's reported result.
Write each as 'what was unknown -> what discovery settled -> what design built on it'. Exact numbers and wording only, no added details, no client quotes beyond the files.
Visual: three-case strip (unknown -> settled -> built).

outline.h2: How long does discovery take inside a full product design engagement?
outline.answerHint: Bold answer: 10-25 working days in our engagement: discovery and product strategy (5-10 days) plus user research (5-15 days), inside the 8-16 week (40-80 working day) digital product design process.
points: Deep link the hub process instead of restating all 5 steps: [our 5-step product design process](/services/digital-product-design-services/#how-does-the-digital-product-design-process-work).

What happens in those days: stakeholder workshops, Jobs to be Done mapping, HEART metrics, interviews with 5-8 users per user group. Then IA and flows (5-10 days) and the prototype round build on the output.
Explain why discovery is built into the engagement rather than sold as a gate: the people who ran the interviews design the screens. Stay within hub wording.
Visual: timeline bar of the 8-16 week engagement with the discovery steps highlighted.

outline.h2: What does a good discovery readout contain?
outline.answerHint: Bold answer: a decision (build, change or stop), the evidence behind it, and outputs a designer can start from. A readout of workshop notes with no users in it is not discovery.
points: Checklist: named target user groups; interview count per group; top findings with quotes; assumption ledger with evidence status; success metrics with baselines or targets; sitemap and core flows; the explicit build/change/stop decision; open questions for the prototype round.

Warning signs: no user interviews (NN/g's 'Are You Doing Real Discoveries?' notes many discoveries lack user research), only stakeholder opinions, no decision, outputs that restate the founder's brief.
Tell the reader to ask any agency for a sample readout before signing.
Visual: readout checklist card (text behind 'Show as text').

outline.h2: How do you scope discovery into a fixed-price proposal?
outline.answerHint: Bold answer: bring your skip-test score, your riskiest 3 assumptions and the number of user groups; those set how many discovery and research days the engagement needs, and the price follows the hub's 4 price factors.
points: Lead angle section. Inputs: skip-test score, top 3 assumptions, user groups and access to users, platforms, launch date.

Price: do not restate the range in full detail; link [what digital product design costs](/services/digital-product-design-services/#how-much-does-digital-product-design-cost) and name the 4 factors from the hub (platforms, user groups, core user flows, validation rounds).
Invitation (natural, specific): send the 3 assumptions to a free consultation, leave with a fixed-scope proposal. Link /contact/. Mention 200+ products since 2017 with a link to /about/.
Use the exact keyword once more here (closing use). Link UP to the hub a second time.

faqs.q: Is a design sprint the same as a discovery phase?
faqs.hint: No. A 5-day design sprint tests 1 direction with 5 users; a discovery phase sets the target users, jobs and success metrics across the product before the design direction is chosen. Do not add a second link to the startups hub here.

faqs.q: Can you skip discovery if you already have a prototype?
faqs.hint: Yes, only if the prototype has been tested with target users and the findings are recent; an untested prototype is an assumption with screens. Point back to the skip test.

faqs.q: What happens if discovery shows the product should not be built?
faqs.hint: You stop or change direction before any code exists, which is the cheapest moment to do it. GOV.UK treats ending after discovery as a valid outcome.

faqs.q: Who from our team needs to join a discovery phase?
faqs.hint: The founder or product owner who makes the decision, 1-2 stakeholders who know customers (sales, support), and an engineer for feasibility questions. Do not invent hour commitments. The startups industry page states 2-4 founder hours per week for startup engagements; do not reuse that figure for this hub.

faqs.q: Does discovery still matter for an AI product?
faqs.hint: Yes. The model choice is a feasibility question, while whether users trust and act on the output is a value and usability question discovery tests. Vocable's interviews shaped every screen of an AI content product (exact wording from the case study only).
